entries.12:11: The young men told him to say his father used whips but he would use scorpions, meaning he would be far harsher. This was a threat of even heavier treatment, not a promise of relief.
entries.12:12: The people came back to Rehoboam on the third day, just as he had told them to. They were expecting his answer to their request.
entries.12:13: Rehoboam answered the people harshly and ignored the wise advice of the older men. He chose to be tough instead of kind.
entries.12:14: Rehoboam repeated the young men's words, telling the people he would make their burden heavier and punish them more severely. He threatened them instead of listening to their pain.
entries.12:15: The king refused to listen to the people, and this happened because God was carrying out what he had planned. God had already said through the prophet Ahijah that Jeroboam would take part of the kingdom.
entries.12:16: When the people saw the king would not listen, they rejected the family of David and went home. They declared they had no share in David's dynasty and would no longer follow Rehoboam.
entries.12:17: Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah. His kingdom was now limited to the southern territory.
entries.12:18: Rehoboam sent Adoniram, who was in charge of forced labor, to the people, and they stoned him to death. Rehoboam quickly fled in his chariot to Jerusalem to save his life.
entries.12:19: From that day on, the people of Israel have been separated from the family of David. The kingdom split, and the northern tribes no longer belonged to David's line.
entries.12:20: When the people heard Jeroboam had returned, they called him to the assembly and made him king over Israel. Only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to the family of David.
entries.12:21: Rehoboam gathered the fighting men of Judah and Benjamin, about 180,000 strong, to go to war against Israel and win back the kingdom. He was preparing for a civil war.
entries.12:22: God spoke to Shemaiah, a man of God, giving him a message. God was about to intervene in the situation.
entries.12:23: God told Shemaiah to deliver the message to Rehoboam, the king of Judah, and to all the people of Judah and Benjamin. The message was for the whole southern kingdom.
entries.12:24: God said they must not go to war against their fellow Israelites, because this division was his plan. The people obeyed God and went home instead of fighting.
entries.12:25: Jeroboam built up the town of Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there, and he also strengthened Penuel. He was securing his new kingdom.
entries.12:26: Jeroboam began to worry that his kingdom would go back to the family of David. He was afraid of losing the people's loyalty.
entries.12:27: Jeroboam feared that if the people kept going to Jerusalem to worship at the Lord's temple, they would turn back to Rehoboam and kill him. He saw worship in Jerusalem as a threat to his rule.
entries.12:28: After thinking it over, Jeroboam made two golden calves and told the people these were the gods who brought them out of Egypt. He set up idols to keep the people from going to Jerusalem.
entries.12:29: Jeroboam placed one golden calf in Bethel and the other in Dan. He set up these idols at two locations in his kingdom.
entries.12:30: This became a sin for Israel, because the people went to worship the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jeroboam led the nation into idol worship.
entries.12:31: Jeroboam built shrines at the high places and appointed priests from ordinary people, not from the tribe of Levi. He changed how worship was done and ignored God's instructions.
entries.12:32: Jeroboam set up a festival in the eighth month, copying the feast in Judah, and he went to the altar in Bethel to offer sacrifices to the golden calves. He created his own religious celebration to compete with Jerusalem.
entries.12:33: Jeroboam went to the altar he had built in Bethel on the day he had chosen himself, and he offered sacrifices and burned incense. He was inventing his own form of worship rather than following God's commands.
entries.13:1: God sent a prophet from Judah to the altar at Bethel, where King Jeroboam was offering sacrifices. It shows God speaks directly into places where worship has gone wrong.
entries.13:2: The prophet announced that a future king named Josiah would one day destroy this false altar and its priests. God was warning that judgment was coming, even if it took years.
entries.13:3: The prophet gave a sign to prove his message was from God: the altar would split and its ashes would spill out. God backs up his words with evidence so people can trust them.
entries.13:4: Jeroboam tried to arrest the prophet, but his outstretched hand froze and he could not pull it back. Opposing God's messenger left the king powerless.
entries.13:5: The altar broke apart and the ashes poured out, exactly as the prophet had said. The sign came true, confirming God's word.
entries.13:6: The king begged the prophet to pray for his hand to be healed, and it was restored. Even a rebellious king could receive mercy when he asked.
entries.13:7: The king invited the prophet home for a meal and a reward. He wanted to soften the prophet and perhaps control him.
entries.13:8: The prophet refused, saying he would not take even half the king's wealth. He was loyal to God's command above any reward.
entries.13:9: God had told him not to eat, drink, or return the same way in that place. Obedience meant following God's instructions exactly.
entries.13:10: So the prophet left by a different road than the one he came on. He kept the command he had been given.
entries.13:11: An old prophet living in Bethel heard from his sons what the man of God had done and said. News of God's work spread quickly.
entries.13:12: The old prophet asked which road the man had taken, and his sons told him. He was curious enough to pursue the visitor.
entries.13:13: The old prophet had his sons saddle a donkey and set off. He was determined to catch up with the man of God.
entries.13:14: He found the man of God resting under an oak tree and confirmed he was the one from Judah. The two prophets met on the road.
entries.13:15: The old prophet invited him back to his house for a meal. It seemed like ordinary hospitality.
entries.13:16: The man of God refused, repeating that God had forbidden him to eat or drink there. He was still trying to obey.
entries.13:17: He explained that God had told him not to eat, drink, or return by the same road. His refusal was based on God's clear command.
entries.13:18: The old prophet lied, claiming an angel had told him to bring the man back for a meal. The man of God was deceived by a false claim.
entries.13:19: So the man of God went back and ate and drank in the old prophet's house. He trusted a lie over what God had already told him.
entries.13:20: While they were at the table, God gave the old prophet a message. God still spoke, even through the man who had lied.
entries.13:21: The old prophet announced that because the man of God had disobeyed God's command, judgment would come. Disobedience had serious consequences.
entries.13:22: He would die and not be buried with his ancestors. His body would be dishonored because he broke God's word.
entries.13:23: After the meal, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the man of God to leave. He sent him back on his way.
entries.13:24: A lion attacked and killed him on the road, and his body lay there with the donkey and the lion beside it. The judgment God announced came true.
entries.13:25: Passersby saw the body and the lion and reported it in the town where the old prophet lived. The news spread to the community.
entries.13:26: The old prophet recognized it as God's judgment on the man who disobeyed. He understood the death as a fulfillment of God's word.
entries.13:27: He told his sons to saddle his donkey, and they did. He was going to retrieve the body.
entries.13:28: He found the body untouched by the lion, and the donkey also unharmed. The lion had killed but not eaten, which was unusual and showed God's hand.
entries.13:29: The old prophet took the body, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back to bury it with mourning. He honored the man of God in death.
entries.13:30: He buried the body in his own tomb and wept over it, calling him brother. Even in judgment, there was grief and respect.
entries.13:31: He told his sons to bury him beside the man of God when he died, so their bones would rest together. He wanted to be associated with the true prophet.
entries.13:32: He was sure the prophecy against the altars in Bethel and Samaria would come true. God's word against false worship would not fail.
entries.13:33: Jeroboam did not change his ways; he kept appointing priests for the false altars from anyone who wanted the job. He hardened his heart despite the warning.
entries.13:34: This became a sin that led to the destruction of Jeroboam's family. Persistent disobedience brought ruin on his house.
entries.14:1: Jeroboam's son Abijah got sick. Even a king's family is not safe from illness and worry.
entries.14:2: Jeroboam told his wife to disguise herself and go to the prophet Ahijah, hoping to get an answer without being recognized. He was trying to hide from the truth he already knew.
entries.14:3: She was to bring simple gifts of bread and honey to the prophet and ask what would happen to the sick boy. People often brought gifts when asking a prophet for God's word.
entries.14:4: She did as her husband said and went to Ahijah's house, but the prophet was now very old and blind. Her disguise might have fooled a blind man, but not God.
entries.14:5: God had already told Ahijah she was coming and that she would pretend to be someone else, and He told him what to say. God sees through every disguise.
entries.14:6: As soon as she came in, Ahijah called her by name and asked why she was pretending, then told her his news was bad. You cannot hide your real self from God.
entries.14:7: God reminded Jeroboam through the prophet that He had raised him from an ordinary man to be ruler over Israel. God's message begins by recalling what He had done for him.
entries.14:8: God said Jeroboam had not been faithful like David, who obeyed God with his whole heart. Being given a position does not excuse unfaithfulness.
entries.14:9: Jeroboam had done more evil than those before him by making other gods and turning his back on the Lord. His sin was serious because he knew better.
entries.14:10: Because of this, God said Jeroboam's whole family line would be cut off and swept away like trash. A leader's sin can bring ruin on his whole household.
entries.14:11: Those of Jeroboam's family who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the country by birds. This was a picture of total disgrace, with no proper burial.
entries.14:12: The prophet sent her home, saying the child would die the moment she entered the town. The answer she came for was the hardest one to hear.
entries.14:13: All Israel would mourn this boy and bury him, because he alone in Jeroboam's family had something good in him before God. Even in judgment, God showed mercy to this child.
entries.14:14: God would soon raise up a new king over Israel who would destroy Jeroboam's family. The judgment would come through a real person at a real time.
entries.14:15: God would shake Israel like a reed in water and uproot them from the land, scattering them beyond the river because of their idols. Persistent idolatry leads to losing what God gave.
entries.14:16: God would give Israel over to trouble because of Jeroboam's sins and because he led the nation into sin. Leaders are accountable for the way they lead others.
entries.14:17: Jeroboam's wife went home to Tirzah, and as she crossed the doorway the child died, just as the prophet said. God's word came true exactly as spoken.
entries.14:18: All Israel buried the boy and mourned him, just as the Lord had said through Ahijah. Even a hard prophecy proved completely reliable.
entries.14:19: The rest of Jeroboam's reign, his wars and his rule, were written in the official records of the kings of Israel. His story is remembered in history.
entries.14:20: Jeroboam ruled twenty-two years, then died and was buried, and his son Nadab became king. No king, however powerful, rules forever.
entries.14:21: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, became king of Judah at forty-one and ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city God had chosen for His name. His mother was Naamah, an Ammonite.
entries.14:22: Judah did evil in God's eyes and made Him angrier than their ancestors had by their sins. Being God's chosen people did not protect them from the results of sin.
entries.14:23: They built shrines, sacred stones, and wooden poles on every high hill and under every green tree. They copied the worship of the nations around them instead of worshiping God.
entries.14:24: There were even people in the land practicing ritual sex in worship of false gods, doing the same disgusting things as the nations God had driven out. Sin had spread into the whole culture.
entries.14:25: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. Judah's sin brought real trouble from a powerful enemy.
entries.14:26: Shishak took all the treasures from the Lord's temple and the king's palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made. The wealth built up in better days was gone in one attack.
entries.14:27: Rehoboam replaced the gold shields with bronze ones and gave them to the guards at the palace door. The replacement showed how far the kingdom's glory had fallen.
entries.14:28: Whenever the king went to the temple, the guards carried the bronze shields and then returned them to their room. It became a routine reminder of what had been lost.
entries.14:29: The rest of Rehoboam's deeds are written in the official records of the kings of Judah. His reign too is part of the recorded history.
entries.14:30: There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their lifetimes. A divided nation meant constant conflict between the two kingdoms.
entries.14:31: Rehoboam died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Abijam became king in his place. His mother's name is mentioned again, and his reign ended like all others.
entries.15:1: Abijam became king of Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's reign over Israel. This dates the change of ruler in the southern kingdom.
entries.15:2: Abijam ruled in Jerusalem for three years, and his mother was Maacah. The text notes his family background.
entries.15:3: Abijam repeated the same sins his father had committed, and his heart was not fully devoted to God like David's was. His example warns us that following a bad family pattern can pull us away from God.
entries.15:4: Even so, God kept a descendant on the throne in Jerusalem because of his promise to David, keeping the city secure. God's faithfulness to his promises does not depend on our goodness.
entries.15:5: David did what was right before God and obeyed him throughout his life, except in the matter of Uriah. This shows that even a faithful person can fail badly, yet God still remembers the overall direction of a life.
entries.15:6: This verse is missing from the text provided, so there is nothing to explain here.
entries.15:7: The rest of Abijam's deeds are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings, and there was ongoing war between him and Jeroboam. The record reminds us that conflict marked this period.
entries.15:8: Abijam died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Asa became king. One king's death makes way for the next.
entries.15:9: Asa became king of Judah in the twentieth year of Jeroboam's reign over Israel. This places Asa's rise within the timeline of the northern kingdom.
entries.15:10: Asa ruled in Jerusalem for forty-one years, and his mother was Maacah. His long reign gave him time to make lasting changes.
entries.15:11: Asa did what was right in God's eyes, following the example of David. His life shows that a person can choose to follow a good example rather than a bad family pattern.
entries.15:12: Asa removed the men involved in shrine prostitution and destroyed the idols his ancestors had made. He took real action to clean up the worship of his nation.
entries.15:13: Asa even removed his own mother from her position as queen because she had made an obscene image for Asherah, and he destroyed it. Doing right may mean confronting people close to us, even family.
entries.15:14: The local worship sites were not removed, but Asa's heart stayed true to God throughout his life. A person can be genuinely devoted to God while still leaving some things unfinished.
entries.15:15: Asa brought the silver, gold, and sacred objects dedicated by his father and himself into the Lord's house. He honored God with valuable gifts.
entries.15:16: There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their reigns. The two kingdoms remained in conflict.
entries.15:17: Baasha attacked Judah and fortified Ramah to cut off all movement in and out of Asa's territory. This was a serious threat to Asa's kingdom.
entries.15:18: Asa took the silver and gold from the Lord's house and his own palace and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, in Damascus. He used sacred treasure to buy help.
entries.15:19: Asa proposed a treaty with Ben-hadad, offering silver and gold to persuade him to break his agreement with Baasha and stop the attacks. He relied on money and foreign alliances rather than on God.
entries.15:20: Ben-hadad agreed and sent his armies against towns in Israel, conquering territory as far as Naphtali. Asa's plan worked, but it came at a cost.
entries.15:21: When Baasha heard what happened, he stopped building Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah. The pressure on Judah eased.
entries.15:22: Asa gathered all Judah and used the stones and wood from Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. He turned the enemy's abandoned materials into defenses for his own land.
entries.15:23: The rest of Asa's deeds and building projects are recorded in Judah's royal history, and in old age he suffered from a disease in his feet. Even a long, mostly good reign ends with weakness and death.
entries.15:24: Asa died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Jehoshaphat became king. The throne passed to the next generation.
entries.15:25: Nadab, Jeroboam's son, became king of Israel in the second year of Asa's reign in Judah and ruled for two years. His time in power was short.
entries.15:26: Nadab did evil in God's eyes, following his father's sinful ways and leading Israel into the same sin. He repeated his father's mistakes instead of learning from them.
entries.15:27: Baasha plotted against Nadab and struck him down at Gibbethon, a Philistine town, while Nadab and Israel's army were besieging it. Even in the middle of a military campaign, betrayal was close at hand.
entries.15:28: Baasha killed Nadab in the third year of Asa's reign and took the throne in his place. This was a violent takeover, not a rightful succession.
entries.15:29: As soon as Baasha became king, he killed every member of Jeroboam's family, fulfilling what the Lord had spoken through the prophet Ahijah. God's word proved true, even through a ruthless man.
entries.15:30: This happened because of Jeroboam's sins and the sins he led Israel into, which provoked the Lord's anger. Persistent sin brought judgment on his whole family.
entries.15:31: The rest of Nadab's deeds are recorded in the official history of Israel's kings. His story is preserved in the records.
entries.15:32: There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their reigns. The conflict between the two kingdoms continued.
entries.15:33: Baasha became king over all Israel in Tirzah in the third year of Asa's reign and ruled for twenty-four years. His reign was long, but it was marked by the same sins.
entries.15:34: Baasha did evil in God's eyes, following Jeroboam's sinful ways and leading Israel into the same sin. A new king did not mean a new direction.
entries.16:1: God sent the prophet Jehu to deliver a message of judgment against King Baasha. It shows that God sees and speaks against those in power who do wrong.
entries.16:2: God reminds Baasha that he raised him from nothing to become king, but Baasha followed Jeroboam's bad example and led Israel into sin. Being given power by God means being accountable to him for how you use it.
entries.16:3: God declares that Baasha's whole family line will be wiped out, just like Jeroboam's was. Persistent sin brings ruin, even on a family.
entries.16:4: Baasha's family members will die shamefully, with their bodies left unburied for dogs and birds. This was a sign of total disgrace in that culture.
entries.16:5: The writer notes that Baasha's other deeds and achievements are recorded in the official royal records. His story is history, but his legacy is judged by his disobedience.
entries.16:6: Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah took the throne. Death comes to every king, and the throne passes on.
entries.16:7: God's judgment on Baasha came through the prophet Jehu because of his evil, his idolatry, and his killing of Jeroboam's family. God holds people responsible even when they repeat sins others started.
entries.16:8: Elah became king of Israel during Asa's reign in Judah and ruled only two years. His short reign hints at how unstable a kingdom built on sin can be.
entries.16:9: Elah's own servant Zimri, a military commander, plotted against him while Elah was drinking heavily at a official's house. Drunkenness and carelessness left him vulnerable to betrayal.
entries.16:10: Zimri attacked and killed Elah, then took the throne himself. This was a violent coup, not a legitimate succession.
entries.16:11: As soon as Zimri took power, he killed every member of Baasha's family and their friends. This fulfilled God's judgment, but Zimri's cruelty was still his own doing.
entries.16:12: Zimri's massacre of Baasha's family fulfilled what God had said through the prophet Jehu. God's word proved true, even through a wicked man's actions.
entries.16:13: The sins of Baasha and Elah, and the way they led Israel into idolatry, provoked God's anger. Leaders who cause others to sin bear a heavy responsibility.
entries.16:14: Elah's other deeds are recorded in the official royal records. His brief reign is summed up and closed.
entries.16:15: Zimri became king for only seven days while the army was away attacking a Philistine town. His reign was short because the army was elsewhere and would soon turn on him.
entries.16:16: When the army heard that Zimri had murdered the king, they proclaimed their commander Omri as king right there in the camp. Loyalty shifted quickly in a crisis.
entries.16:17: Omri marched the army back and surrounded Tirzah to take the city from Zimri. Zimri's coup was doomed from the start.
entries.16:18: When Zimri saw the city was lost, he set the palace on fire and died in the flames. His rebellion ended in self-destruction.
entries.16:19: Zimri died because of his own sin and because he followed Jeroboam's idolatry and led Israel into it. His death was a judgment on his evil.
entries.16:20: Zimri's other deeds and his plot are recorded in the official royal records. His brief, violent reign is remembered as a warning.
entries.16:21: Israel split into two factions, half supporting Tibni and half supporting Omri. Political division followed the chaos of repeated coups.
entries.16:22: Omri's supporters defeated Tibni's side, and Tibni and his brother died, leaving Omri as king. Power was settled by force, not by God's choice.
entries.16:23: Omri became king over Israel during Asa's reign and ruled twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. His reign was longer and more stable than the kings just before him.
entries.16:24: Omri bought a hill from Shemer for silver and built a city there, naming it Samaria after the seller. This city became the new capital of the northern kingdom.
entries.16:25: Omri did more evil than any king before him. Even a strong, successful ruler can be judged by God for his disobedience.
entries.16:26: Omri copied Jeroboam's idolatry and led Israel into the same sins, making God angry. Following a bad example multiplies the harm.
entries.16:27: Omri's other deeds and his military strength are recorded in the official royal records. His accomplishments are noted, but so is his evil.
entries.16:28: Omri died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab became king. The throne passed to a son who would be even worse.
entries.16:29: Ahab became king over Israel during Asa's reign and ruled twenty-two years in Samaria. His long reign would bring deep spiritual decline.
entries.16:30: Ahab did more evil than any king before him. Each generation that ignores God's warnings tends to sink further.
entries.16:31: Ahab treated Jeroboam's sins as minor and then married Jezebel, a foreign princess, and began to worship and serve the false god Baal. Marrying into idolatry pulled him and the nation further from God.
entries.16:32: Ahab built a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria. He officially established idol worship in the capital of Israel.
entries.16:33: Ahab made an idol for the goddess Asherah and provoked God more than any king before him. He didn't just tolerate idolatry; he promoted it.
entries.16:34: During Ahab's reign, a man named Hiel rebuilt Jericho and lost his oldest and youngest sons in the process, just as Joshua had prophesied. God's word spoken long before came true, showing that his warnings are not empty.
entries.17:1: Elijah tells King Ahab that because Israel has turned from God, there will be no rain until Elijah says so. It shows that God's word, spoken through an ordinary man, controls even the weather.
entries.17:2: God speaks directly to Elijah to guide him. It reminds the reader that God still gives personal direction to those who serve him.
entries.17:3: God tells Elijah to leave and hide by a stream east of the Jordan. Sometimes God's protection means stepping away from the public eye and waiting on him.
entries.17:4: God promises Elijah that the stream will supply his water and that ravens will bring him food. It shows God can provide in surprising, even unlikely, ways.
entries.17:5: Elijah simply obeys and goes to the stream as God commanded. Trusting God's word enough to act on it is the heart of faith.
entries.17:6: The ravens actually bring Elijah bread and meat each morning and evening, and he drinks from the stream. God keeps his promise in a way no one would expect.
entries.17:7: Eventually the stream dries up because the drought Elijah announced has taken hold. Even when God's provision changes, he is still in control of the circumstances.
entries.17:8: God speaks to Elijah again after the stream dries up. God's guidance often comes just when the previous plan runs out.
entries.17:9: God sends Elijah to a foreign town and says a widow there will feed him. God's care reaches beyond Israel, and he uses ordinary, needy people to provide.
entries.17:10: Elijah arrives and asks a widow gathering firewood for a drink of water. It's a simple request that opens the door to a much bigger story of God's provision.
entries.17:11: Elijah also asks her for a piece of bread. He is asking someone who has almost nothing, which sets up a test of trust.
entries.17:12: The widow swears she has only a handful of flour and a little oil left, and she is preparing a final meal for herself and her son before they starve. Her honesty shows how desperate her situation is.
entries.17:13: Elijah tells her not to be afraid and asks her to feed him first, then make food for herself and her son. It's a bold request that calls her to trust God's promise before seeing the result.
entries.17:14: God promises that her flour and oil will not run out until the rain comes. The promise is specific and tied to God's timing, not hers.
entries.17:15: The widow does what Elijah says, and she, Elijah, and her household eat for many days. Her obedience, though risky, leads to survival for everyone.
entries.17:16: The flour and oil keep lasting exactly as God promised through Elijah. It confirms that God's word through his prophet can be trusted.
entries.17:17: Later the widow's son becomes so sick that he stops breathing. Even after a miracle, life still brings pain and loss.
entries.17:18: The widow blames Elijah, thinking her son's death is punishment for some sin. Grief often makes people look for someone or something to blame.
entries.17:19: Elijah calmly takes the boy from her, carries him upstairs, and lays him on his own bed. He responds to her panic with action rather than argument.
entries.17:20: Elijah cries out to God, asking why this tragedy has come to the widow who took him in. He brings his confusion and pain honestly to God in prayer.
entries.17:21: Elijah stretches himself over the child three times and pleads with God to bring the boy back to life. It shows persistent, earnest prayer for something only God can do.
entries.17:22: God hears Elijah's prayer, and the boy's life returns and he revives. God is shown to have power over death itself.
entries.17:23: Elijah brings the living boy back downstairs and gives him to his mother. The miracle restores not just the child but the mother's hope.
entries.17:24: The widow declares that she now knows Elijah is truly a man of God and that his words are true. Seeing God act in her own home moved her from doubt to confidence.
entries.18:1: After a long drought, God told Elijah it was time to show himself to King Ahab because God was about to send rain. It reminds the reader that God keeps his timing and his promises.
entries.18:2: Elijah obeyed and went to meet Ahab, even though the famine in Samaria was severe. It shows that doing what God says can mean stepping into hard situations.
entries.18:3: Ahab called for Obadiah, the man who managed his palace, who deeply respected and feared the Lord. It shows that faith in God can exist even inside a corrupt king's household.
entries.18:4: When Queen Jezebel was killing God's prophets, Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them. It shows quiet courage and loyalty to God when it was dangerous to be faithful.
entries.18:5: Ahab told Obadiah they should search the whole land for water and grass to keep their horses and animals alive. It shows how desperate the drought had made everyone, even the king.
entries.18:6: The two men split up and searched the country in different directions. It simply sets the scene for Obadiah's unexpected meeting with Elijah.
entries.18:7: Obadiah ran into Elijah and fell face down in respect, asking if it was really him. It shows how greatly Elijah was respected, and how startling his sudden appearance was.
entries.18:8: Elijah confirmed it was him and told Obadiah to go tell Ahab that he had arrived. It was a simple but risky instruction that put Obadiah in a hard spot.
entries.18:9: Obadiah asked what he had done wrong to be sent on an errand that could get him killed. It shows his very real fear of the king's anger.
entries.18:10: Obadiah swore that Ahab had searched every nation for Elijah and made people swear they hadn't seen him. It shows how determined the king was to find Elijah.
entries.18:11: Obadiah pointed out that Elijah was now asking him to simply announce his arrival to the king. He was worried about what would happen next.
entries.18:12: Obadiah feared that God's Spirit would whisk Elijah away and Ahab would blame and kill him, despite his lifelong devotion to God. It shows how fear can make even faithful people hesitate.
entries.18:13: Obadiah reminded Elijah that he had hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel and fed them. He was pleading his own record of faithfulness as proof he deserved not to be put in danger.
entries.18:14: Obadiah repeated his fear that telling Ahab would cost him his life. It shows how heavy the pressure felt to him.
entries.18:15: Elijah swore by the living God that he would definitely show himself to Ahab that very day. His firm promise was meant to calm Obadiah's fear.
entries.18:16: Obadiah went and told Ahab, and Ahab went out to meet Elijah. The long-awaited confrontation was finally about to happen.
entries.18:17: When Ahab saw Elijah, he accused him of being the one who brought trouble on Israel. It shows how people often blame God's messengers for problems their own choices caused.
entries.18:18: Elijah shot back that the trouble came from Ahab and his family, because they had abandoned God's commands and followed false gods. It shows that the real cause of Israel's trouble was their own unfaithfulness.
entries.18:19: Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel and the 450 prophets of Baal at Mount Carmel for a showdown. It was a public challenge to settle who really was God.
entries.18:20: Ahab did as Elijah said and gathered the people and the prophets at Mount Carmel. The stage was set for a dramatic test.
entries.18:21: Elijah asked the crowd how long they would keep wavering between two loyalties, and told them to choose plainly whether God or Baal was real. The people stayed silent, showing their confusion or unwillingness to decide.
entries.18:22: Elijah pointed out that he stood alone as God's prophet while Baal had 450 prophets. The odds looked completely against him, which made what followed even more striking.
entries.18:23: Elijah proposed a test: each side would prepare an ox on wood but light no fire. It was a fair and simple setup that would let the true God reveal himself.
entries.18:24: Each side would pray to their god, and whichever one answered with fire would prove to be the real God, and the people agreed this was fair. It put the question of who is truly God to a clear test.
entries.18:25: Elijah let the many prophets of Baal go first and call on their god, with no fire lit under the offering. It gave them every chance to prove their god was real.
entries.18:26: The prophets of Baal cried out to him from morning until noon and danced around the altar, but nothing happened. Their god gave no answer at all.
entries.18:27: At midday Elijah mocked them, suggesting their god might be thinking, busy, traveling, or asleep and needed waking. It highlighted how powerless a made-up god really is.
entries.18:28: They shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and swords until blood flowed, as their custom was. It shows how frantic and empty their worship had become.
entries.18:29: They kept praying until the time of the evening offering, but there was still no voice, no answer, and no one paying attention. Their god simply could not respond.
entries.18:30: Elijah called the people to come close and rebuilt the altar of the Lord that had been torn down. He was restoring proper worship before asking God to act.
entries.18:31: Elijah used twelve stones, one for each tribe of Jacob's sons, whom God had named Israel. It was a visual reminder that all twelve tribes belonged to God.
entries.18:32: He built the altar in the Lord's name and dug a deep trench around it. The trench would make the coming miracle even more unmistakable.
entries.18:33: Elijah arranged the wood, laid the cut-up ox on it, and told them to pour four jars of water over the offering and wood. He was making it impossible for anyone to claim he secretly started a fire.
entries.18:34: He told them to do it a second and then a third time, and they did. The offering was now thoroughly soaked.
entries.18:35: The water ran all around the altar and filled the trench. Everything was drenched, setting up an even more dramatic display of God's power.
entries.18:36: At the time of the evening offering, Elijah prayed to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, asking him to show that he is God and that Elijah acted on his orders. He wanted the glory to go to God, not himself.
entries.18:37: Elijah begged God to answer so the people would see that he is God and that he was turning their hearts back to him. His prayer was focused on the people's restoration.
entries.18:38: Fire from the Lord fell and burned up the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and even the water in the trench. It was an overwhelming answer that left no doubt about God's power.
entries.18:39: When the people saw it, they fell on their faces and declared that the Lord is God. The miracle brought them to acknowledge the truth openly.
entries.18:40: Elijah ordered that none of Baal's prophets escape, and they were taken to the Kishon stream and put to death there. It was a harsh act of removing the false worship that had led Israel astray.
entries.18:41: Elijah tells King Ahab to go eat and drink because he can hear the sound of heavy rain coming. It means God was about to keep his promise, so the reader can trust that God's word comes true even before we see anything.
entries.18:42: Ahab goes off to eat, but Elijah climbs to the top of Mount Carmel and bends down with his face to the ground to pray. It shows that the one who spoke about the rain now humbly waits on God for it, and it invites the reader to pray with humble persistence.
entries.18:43: Elijah sends his servant to look toward the sea for rain, and the servant reports nothing, so Elijah keeps sending him back seven times. It means real faith keeps waiting even when nothing appears yet, and it encourages the reader not to give up too soon.
entries.18:44: On the seventh look the servant sees a tiny cloud the size of a hand, and Elijah immediately tells Ahab to hitch up his chariot and leave before the rain traps him. It shows that God's answer can start very small, and the reader is reminded to act on what God begins.
entries.18:45: Soon the sky turns black with wind and clouds and a huge rainstorm pours down, and Ahab rides off to Jezreel. It means the drought really ended just as God said, showing the reader that God's promises are fulfilled completely.
entries.18:46: God's power comes on Elijah, and he tucks up his robe and runs ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel. It shows God giving unusual strength for the moment, reminding the reader that God equips people to do what he asks.
entries.19:1: Ahab told his wife Jezebel everything Elijah had done, including how he had killed all the prophets of Baal. This shows that the powerful people in charge now knew what Elijah had done and would react to it.
entries.19:2: Jezebel sent a message to Elijah swearing that by the next day she would kill him, just as he had killed her prophets. She was threatening his life directly and making it clear she meant it.
entries.19:3: Elijah was afraid and ran for his life, traveling all the way to Beersheba in Judah, where he left his servant behind. Even a brave prophet can be scared enough to flee when someone threatens to kill him.
entries.19:4: Elijah went alone into the desert, sat under a bush, and asked God to let him die, saying he had had enough and was no better than his ancestors. He was deeply discouraged and worn out, and he told God exactly how he felt.
entries.19:5: He lay down and fell asleep, and an angel touched him and told him to get up and eat. God cared for Elijah's physical needs before dealing with his despair.
entries.19:6: Elijah looked and saw bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water beside his head, so he ate and drank and lay down again. God gave him simple, practical help right where he was.
entries.19:7: The angel came back a second time, touched him, and told him to eat because the journey ahead would be too much for him. God knew Elijah needed more rest and food before he could keep going.
entries.19:8: Elijah got up, ate and drank, and then traveled forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, strengthened by that food. God can sustain a tired person for a long and difficult road.
entries.19:9: At the mountain Elijah spent the night in a cave, and God spoke to him, asking what he was doing there. God invites Elijah to explain himself and starts a conversation with him.
entries.19:10: Elijah said he had been completely devoted to God, but the Israelites had broken their covenant, destroyed God's altars, and killed his prophets, leaving him alone and now hunted. He felt like the only faithful person left and was afraid for his life.
entries.19:11: God told Elijah to stand on the mountain, and a powerful wind tore the rocks apart, then an earthquake came, but God was not in either one. God's presence was not shown through dramatic, destructive forces.
entries.19:12: After the earthquake came a fire, but God was not in the fire either; then came a quiet, gentle sound. God often speaks in a still, small way rather than through loud and frightening events.
entries.19:13: When Elijah heard the gentle sound, he covered his face with his cloak and stood at the cave entrance, and a voice asked him again what he was doing there. Elijah responded with reverence to God's quiet presence.
entries.19:14: Elijah gave the same answer as before: he had been devoted to God, but the people had broken their covenant, destroyed the altars, and killed the prophets, and now he was alone and they wanted to kill him. He still felt isolated and afraid, even after encountering God.
entries.19:15: God told Elijah to go back through the desert to Damascus and anoint Hazael as king over Aram. God gave Elijah a clear job to do instead of letting him stay stuck in despair.
entries.19:16: God also told him to anoint Jehu as king over Israel and Elisha as prophet to take Elijah's place. God was providing for the future and making sure the work would continue after Elijah.
entries.19:17: God said that those who escaped Hazael's sword would be killed by Jehu, and those who escaped Jehu's sword would be killed by Elisha. God was telling Elijah that judgment on the unfaithful would surely come through these leaders.
entries.19:18: God told Elijah that he had kept seven thousand people in Israel who had never bowed to Baal or kissed his image. Elijah was not alone after all; God had many faithful people he did not know about.
entries.19:19: Elijah left and found Elisha plowing with twelve pairs of oxen, and Elijah threw his cloak over him. This was a sign that Elisha was being called to follow and eventually take Elijah's place.
entries.19:20: Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and asked to say goodbye to his parents first; Elijah told him to go back, since he had not forced him. Elisha was allowed to settle things at home before beginning his new calling.
entries.19:21: Elisha went back, slaughtered the oxen, cooked them over the wooden plows, and fed the people, then followed Elijah and served him. He left his old life completely and committed himself to the work God had called him to.
entries.20:1: Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, gathered a huge army with many allies and attacked Samaria, the capital of Israel, and surrounded it. It means the people of Israel were facing a powerful enemy with no easy way out.
entries.20:2: Ben-hadad sent messengers into the city to deliver his demands to King Ahab. It means the threat was not distant; it came right to the king's door.
entries.20:3: Ben-hadad demanded Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children as his own. It means he was not just asking for tribute but for total surrender of everything Ahab valued.
entries.20:4: Ahab answered that he accepted Ben-hadad's terms and would give him everything he had. It means Ahab was willing to give up almost anything to avoid a fight.
entries.20:5: Ben-hadad's messengers returned with a stronger demand, repeating the claim on Ahab's wealth and family. It means the first concession was not enough; the enemy wanted more.
entries.20:6: Ben-hadad said his men would come the next day and search through the houses, taking anything they found valuable. It means the threat had moved from a demand to an actual plan to plunder the city.
entries.20:7: Ahab called the elders of the land and pointed out that Ben-hadad was looking for trouble, since he had already agreed to give up his family and wealth. It means Ahab recognized the demand was a trap and wanted the leaders to see it too.
entries.20:8: The elders and the people told Ahab not to listen to Ben-hadad or do what he asked. It means the leaders of Israel stood with their king and refused to surrender further.
entries.20:9: Ahab told Ben-hadad's messengers that he would keep the first agreement but could not accept this new demand. It means Ahab drew a line and refused to give in completely.
entries.20:10: Ben-hadad replied with a boast that he would reduce Samaria to dust, swearing by his gods. It means he was threatening total destruction and mocking Israel's ability to resist.
entries.20:11: Ahab answered that a man should not boast while still putting on his armor, but only after the battle is won. It means Ahab was saying Ben-hadad should not brag before the fight even started.
entries.20:12: Ben-hadad heard the answer while drinking with his allied kings and ordered his men to get ready to attack the city. It means the boast turned into action, and the battle was about to begin.
entries.20:13: A prophet came to Ahab and told him that God would give the huge enemy army into his hands that day, so Ahab would know that God is the Lord. It means God was going to act on Israel's behalf even though Ahab had not been faithful.
entries.20:14: Ahab asked who would do the fighting, and the prophet said it would be the young servants of the district leaders, with Ahab leading them. It means God would use unlikely, ordinary people to win the battle.
entries.20:15: Ahab gathered the 232 young servants of the district leaders and then the rest of the army, seven thousand men. It means Israel's force was small compared to the enemy, making the coming victory clearly God's doing.
entries.20:16: Israel's men went out at midday while Ben-hadad was still drinking in his tent with his thirty-two allied kings. It means the enemy was caught off guard and unprepared.
entries.20:17: The young servants of the district leaders went out first, and Ben-hadad sent scouts who reported that men were coming out of Samaria. It means the attack began with a small advance group.
entries.20:18: Ben-hadad ordered his men to capture the attackers alive, whether they came for peace or for war. It means he underestimated them and wanted prisoners rather than a real fight.
entries.20:19: The young servants went out of the city with the rest of the army following behind them. It means Israel advanced in force, not just a small raiding party.
entries.20:20: Each Israelite soldier killed his opponent, and the Arameans fled with Israel chasing them, while Ben-hadad escaped on horseback with his cavalry. It means the battle turned into a rout, and the enemy king barely got away.
entries.20:21: The king of Israel went out and captured the enemy's horses and chariots and struck down many Arameans. It means Israel won a decisive victory and took the enemy's military equipment.
entries.20:22: The prophet told Ahab to strengthen himself and be careful, because a year later the king of Aram would attack again. It means the victory was not the end; trouble was coming back.
entries.20:23: Ben-hadad's servants said Israel's god was a god of the hills, which is why Israel won, but if they fought in the lowlands they would win. It means they misunderstood God as limited to certain places.
entries.20:24: They advised Ben-hadad to remove the kings from their command positions and replace them with trained captains. It means they wanted a more professional army for the next battle.
entries.20:25: They told him to raise another army just like the one that was destroyed, with the same number of horses and chariots, and fight Israel in the lowlands where they expected to win. It means they planned to try again on their own terms.
entries.20:26: A year later Ben-hadad gathered the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. It means the predicted attack happened exactly as the prophet said.
entries.20:27: Israel gathered and prepared food, then went out against them; Israel's camp looked like two small flocks of goats compared to the land full of Arameans. It means Israel was badly outnumbered.
entries.20:28: A man of God told Ahab that because the Arameans said the Lord is only a god of the hills and not the valleys, God would give the whole army into Israel's hands, so they would know He is the Lord. It means God would prove He rules everywhere, not just in one kind of place.
entries.20:29: The two armies faced each other for seven days, and on the seventh day Israel killed a hundred thousand Aramean foot soldiers in one day. It means the battle was a massive defeat for the enemy.
entries.20:30: The rest fled into Aphek, where a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of them, and Ben-hadad hid in an inner room in the city. It means the enemy's refuge became a death trap, and their king was left hiding.
entries.20:31: Ben-hadad's servants suggested they wear rough cloth and ropes and surrender to Israel's king, since they had heard the kings of Israel were merciful, hoping he would spare Ben-hadad's life. It means they were desperate and appealing for mercy.
entries.20:32: They came to Ahab in mourning clothes and ropes and asked him to spare Ben-hadad's life, and Ahab replied that Ben-hadad was still alive and called him his brother. It means Ahab was ready to treat his enemy as a friend.
entries.20:33: The men seized on Ahab's word and confirmed that Ben-hadad was his brother, so Ahab ordered him brought out and had him come up into his chariot. It means Ahab welcomed his defeated enemy with honor.
entries.20:34: Ben-hadad offered to return towns his father had taken and let Ahab set up trading streets in Damascus, and Ahab made a treaty with him and let him go. It means Ahab made a deal with the enemy instead of treating him as God's defeated foe.
entries.20:35: A member of the prophets' group told his neighbor, by the word of the Lord, to strike him, but the man refused. It means the man disobeyed a direct command from God given through a prophet.
entries.20:36: The prophet told him that because he did not obey the Lord's voice, a lion would kill him as soon as he left, and that is what happened. It means disobeying God's word brought serious consequences.
entries.20:37: The prophet met another man and asked him to strike him, and this man did, wounding him. It means this time the command was obeyed.
entries.20:38: The prophet went and covered his face with his headband and stood by the road waiting for the king to pass. It means he disguised himself to deliver a message to Ahab.
entries.20:39: As the king passed, the prophet called out a story about a soldier who was given a prisoner to guard, with his own life or a large amount of silver as the penalty if the prisoner escaped. It means he was setting up a lesson for the king to judge.
entries.20:40: The prophet said that while he was busy looking around, the prisoner got away, and the king replied that he had judged himself guilty and must pay the penalty. It means Ahab pronounced the verdict without realizing it applied to him.
entries.20:41: The prophet dropped his disguise and let the king see who he really was. It means the truth we try to hide from eventually gets shown to us, so it's better to face it honestly.
entries.20:42: God says the king will pay with his own life and his people's lives because he spared the enemy God had condemned. It means disobeying God's clear command has real consequences, even for powerful people.
entries.20:43: The king went home sullen and furious about the sentence against him. It means he was angry at the outcome rather than sorry for what he did, and that stubborn anger kept him from God.
entries.21:1: Naboth owned a vineyard right next to King Ahab's palace in Jezreel. It was his family's land, and it mattered because it sat close to the king's property.
entries.21:2: Ahab offered Naboth a fair deal—a better vineyard or cash—so he could turn the land into a vegetable garden near his house. It sounds reasonable, but Ahab was used to getting what he wanted.
entries.21:3: Naboth refused because the land was his family's inherited property, which in Israel was not supposed to be sold permanently. He chose loyalty to his family and God's law over pleasing the king.
entries.21:4: Ahab went home sulking, angry that he didn't get his way, and lay in bed refusing to eat. A grown king acted like a spoiled child because one man said no.
entries.21:5: Jezebel, Ahab's wife, noticed he was sulking and asked why he wouldn't eat. She was about to take charge of the situation.
entries.21:6: Ahab explained that Naboth had refused to sell or trade the vineyard. He left out that Naboth had a legitimate reason rooted in his family's inheritance.
entries.21:7: Jezebel basically said, "You're the king—act like it," and promised to get the vineyard for him herself. She was willing to use royal power to take what was not hers.
entries.21:8: Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his official seal, sending them to the town leaders where Naboth lived. She used the king's authority to set a trap.
entries.21:9: She told the leaders to call a public fast and put Naboth in a place of honor at the front. The setup made it look like a solemn religious occasion.
entries.21:10: She arranged for two worthless men to falsely accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king, a crime punishable by stoning. It was a deliberate, calculated plot to kill an innocent man.
entries.21:11: The town leaders did exactly what Jezebel's letters said, without questioning or objecting. They went along with an evil plan because it came from the palace.
entries.21:12: They proclaimed a fast and gave Naboth a prominent seat, making the coming accusation look official and serious. The whole town was drawn into the scheme.
entries.21:13: The two false witnesses accused Naboth of cursing God and the king, and he was dragged outside town and stoned to death. An innocent man died because of lies and corrupt leaders.
entries.21:14: They reported back to Jezebel that Naboth was dead. The murder was complete, and she had gotten what she wanted.
entries.21:15: Jezebel told Ahab to go and take the vineyard now that Naboth was dead. She presented the murder as good news and a done deal.
entries.21:16: Ahab went straight to the vineyard to claim it, showing he was willing to benefit from the crime. He took the land without a word of concern for the man who died.
entries.21:17: God spoke to the prophet Elijah, setting up a confrontation with Ahab. God had seen what happened and was not silent.
entries.21:18: God told Elijah to go find Ahab in Naboth's vineyard, where he had gone to take possession. Ahab thought he had gotten away with it, but God knew exactly where he was.
entries.21:19: God's message was blunt: Ahab had murdered a man to take his land, and he would pay with his own life—dogs would lick his blood in the same place. The judgment matched the crime.
entries.21:20: Ahab greeted Elijah with hostility, calling him an enemy, and Elijah answered that Ahab had brought this on himself by doing evil. Ahab's real problem was not Elijah but his own choices.
entries.21:21: God announced that Ahab's entire family line would be wiped out—every male descendant would be cut off. The judgment was total because Ahab's evil was persistent.
entries.21:22: God said Ahab's family would end like the families of Jeroboam and Baasha, earlier kings whose dynasties were destroyed for their sins. Ahab had made God angry and led Israel into evil.
entries.21:23: God also pronounced judgment on Jezebel: she would be eaten by dogs in Jezreel. The one who plotted murder would meet a shameful end.
entries.21:24: Any member of Ahab's family who died in the city would be eaten by dogs, and any who died in the country would be eaten by birds. This meant none of them would get a proper burial—a sign of disgrace.
entries.21:25: The writer notes that no one was as thoroughly evil as Ahab, and that Jezebel pushed him into it. Ahab was not just weak; he willingly gave himself over to evil.
entries.21:26: Ahab did disgusting things by worshiping false gods, copying the wicked practices of the Amorites whom God had driven out. He sank lower than the nations around him.
entries.21:27: When Ahab heard the judgment, he genuinely humbled himself—wearing rough cloth, fasting, and walking around quietly. He showed real grief and repentance, at least outwardly.
entries.21:28: God spoke to Elijah again after Ahab's humble response. God noticed the change in Ahab's behavior.
entries.21:29: God told Elijah that because Ahab had humbled himself, the disaster would not come during his lifetime but during his son's reign. God showed mercy in delaying judgment, though the evil was not left unpunished.
entries.22:1: For three years the two kingdoms stayed at peace instead of fighting. Quiet seasons are part of the story too, not just the battles.
entries.22:2: In that third year, Judah's king Jehoshaphat traveled to visit Israel's king. This visit sets up a partnership between the two kings.
entries.22:3: Israel's king pointed out that a border town belonged to them but they had done nothing to take it back. He was stirring up his officials to act.
entries.22:4: The king asked Jehoshaphat to join the fight, and Jehoshaphat agreed to share everything he had. It's generous loyalty, though he commits before asking God.
entries.22:5: Jehoshaphat wisely said they should first ask God what to do. Even when plans seem obvious, it's right to seek God's direction.
entries.22:6: The king gathered about four hundred prophets, and they all said to go and that God would give victory. A crowd agreeing doesn't prove they speak for God.
entries.22:7: Jehoshaphat wasn't satisfied with the crowd and asked if there was another prophet of the Lord. He wanted a genuine word from God, not just confirmation.
entries.22:8: The king admitted there was one prophet, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never predicted good. Jehoshaphat gently corrected him, showing we shouldn't reject truth just because it's unwelcome.
entries.22:9: The king sent an official to bring Micaiah quickly. Despite his dislike, he still summoned the prophet.
entries.22:10: The two kings sat in royal robes at the city gate while all the prophets performed before them. It was an impressive display of royal power and religious excitement.
entries.22:11: One prophet made iron horns and declared that with them the king would crush the enemy completely. It was a dramatic, confident prediction of victory.
entries.22:12: All the prophets echoed the same message: go and succeed, because God will give victory. Their unity made the advice seem certain.
entries.22:13: The messenger urged Micaiah to agree with the other prophets and speak favorably. He was pressuring him to go along with the crowd.
entries.22:14: Micaiah promised to say only what the Lord told him, no matter what others said. That's the mark of a true prophet: loyalty to God's word over popularity.
entries.22:15: Micaiah first repeated the prophets' words, likely in a mocking tone. The king sensed he wasn't being serious and demanded the truth.
entries.22:16: The king made Micaiah swear to tell him only the truth in God's name. He wanted honesty, even if he wouldn't like it.
entries.22:17: Micaiah described Israel scattered like sheep with no shepherd, meaning the king would die and the people would go home. The picture spelled disaster for the king.
entries.22:18: The king turned to Jehoshaphat and said this proved Micaiah only ever predicted bad things for him. He heard the warning but only complained about the messenger.
entries.22:19: Micaiah then described a vision of the Lord on his throne with all heaven's army around him. He was claiming a direct, authoritative word from God.
entries.22:20: In the vision, the Lord asked how Ahab could be drawn into going to his death at Ramoth-gilead, and various spirits offered ideas. The scene shows God sovereignly directing events.
entries.22:21: A spirit stepped forward before the Lord and volunteered to trick Ahab. Even deceptive plans are shown as under God's control.
entries.22:22: The spirit proposed to be a lying influence in the mouths of Ahab's prophets, and the Lord permitted it. Ahab's own preference for flattery left him open to deception.
entries.22:23: Micaiah concluded that God had allowed a lying spirit in these prophets and had decreed disaster for Ahab. The false comfort was itself part of the judgment.
entries.22:24: Zedekiah slapped Micaiah and mocked him, asking where God's spirit had gone. The false prophet responded to truth with violence.
entries.22:25: Micaiah warned that Zedekiah would see the truth when he hid in an inner room for safety. His confidence would collapse when events proved Micaiah right.
entries.22:26: The king ordered Micaiah taken back to the city officials. He was silencing the prophet rather than listening to the warning.
entries.22:27: Micaiah was to be jailed and fed meager prison rations until the king returned safely. The king was betting his own safety against God's word.
entries.22:28: Micaiah said that if the king returned safely, God had not spoken through him. He staked his credibility on the prophecy coming true.
entries.22:29: Both kings went up to Ramoth-gilead to fight, ignoring the warning. They proceeded with the plan despite the clear word from God.
entries.22:30: Ahab disguised himself as an ordinary soldier while Jehoshaphat wore royal robes. Ahab tried to dodge the prophecy by hiding his identity.
entries.22:31: The enemy king ordered his chariot commanders to target only the king of Israel. The battle was aimed squarely at Ahab.
entries.22:32: The chariot commanders mistook Jehoshaphat for Ahab and surrounded him, but he cried out. He was in danger only because he had joined a fight God had warned against.
entries.22:33: When they realized Jehoshaphat wasn't the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him. God spared him, though he had put himself in harm's way.
entries.22:34: A soldier shot an arrow at random, and it struck Ahab in a gap in his armor. The disguised king was hit anyway, showing no disguise can escape God's word.
entries.22:35: The battle raged on while Ahab was propped up in his chariot, bleeding into it, until he died by evening. The prophecy came true despite all his precautions.
entries.22:36: At sunset a cry went through the army telling everyone to go home because the king was dead. The scattered sheep of Micaiah's vision went back to their towns.
entries.22:37: They brought Ahab's body to Samaria and buried him there. The king who tried to avoid his fate was laid to rest in his own city.
entries.22:38: When his chariot was washed at a pool in Samaria, dogs licked up his blood, just as the Lord had said. The prophecy was fulfilled down to the smallest detail.
entries.22:39: The writer notes that the rest of Ahab's achievements, including his ivory palace and building projects, are recorded in the royal records. His impressive legacy is summed up in a history book.
entries.22:40: Ahab died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king. One king's story ended and the next began, as God's word had foretold.
entries.22:41: Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah during the fourth year that Ahab ruled Israel. This dates his reign and shows the two kingdoms were being tracked side by side.
entries.22:42: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he took the throne and ruled twenty-five years in Jerusalem; his mother was Azubah. These details identify him and mark the length of his reign.
entries.22:43: He followed his father Asa's example and did what pleased the Lord, but he left the local worship sites standing, so people kept offering sacrifices there. He was faithful overall, yet his reforms were incomplete.
entries.22:44: Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel. This kept the northern and southern kingdoms from fighting each other during his reign.
entries.22:45: The other things Jehoshaphat did, including his power and wars, are recorded in the official history of Judah's kings. His full story is preserved elsewhere, not in this book.
entries.22:46: He removed from the land the remaining men who had been used in pagan worship, including those left over from his father Asa's time. He carried on cleaning out practices that dishonored God.
entries.22:47: At that time Edom had no king of its own. This note sets the political situation around Judah's neighbor.
entries.22:48: Jehoshaphat had ships built to sail to Ophir for gold, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber before they could go. His plan for trade and wealth failed.
entries.22:49: Ahaziah son of Ahab offered to send his men along with Jehoshaphat's sailors, but Jehoshaphat refused. He declined the partnership with Israel's king.
entries.22:50: Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Jehoram became king after him. His reign ended and passed to the next generation.
entries.22:51: Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in Jehoshaphat's seventeenth year, and he ruled only two years. His short reign is dated against Judah's king.
entries.22:52: Ahaziah did what was evil in the Lord's sight, following the bad examples of his parents and of Jeroboam, who led Israel into sin. He repeated the same wrong patterns as those before him.
entries.22:53: He served and worshiped Baal, which angered the Lord, the God of Israel, just as his father had done. His idolatry provoked God and continued his family's unfaithfulness.
